```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

```{r load-packages}
library(tidyverse)
library(naniar)
library(tidymodels)

options(bdat602.source_only = TRUE)
source("courses/bdat-602/_teacher/resources/datasets/simulate_bdat602_data.R")
health_data <- simulate_bdat602(n = 500000, seed = 602)
```

## Task 1: Visualise missingness

```{r task1-vis-miss}
vis_miss(health_data |> select(bmi, income, complaint_notes, days_since_last_claim))
```

```{r task1-summary}
cat("Total missing cells:", n_miss(health_data), "\n")
cat("Overall % missing:  ", round(pct_miss(health_data), 2), "%\n")
```

## Task 2: Classify each missing variable

```{r task2-classify}
# bmi: MAR — the simulator links BMI missingness to point-of-sale data collection.
#   Younger policyholders (who buy online without an in-person check-up) are more
#   likely to have BMI unrecorded. Missingness depends on age (observed), not on
#   BMI itself — so this is MAR.

# income: MNAR — individuals with very high or very low incomes are more likely to
#   decline to disclose. The probability of missingness is related to the income value
#   itself (the missing variable), making this MNAR. Simple median imputation will
#   underestimate average income.

# complaint_notes: MCAR — 10% of records have no complaint note because no complaint
#   was lodged. Whether a note is missing is unrelated to any other variable.
#   (Structurally, this is "missingness by design" — no complaint = no note.)

# days_since_last_claim: MCAR (structural) — records with num_claims = 0 have
#   no claim date by definition. The additional 2% random missing among claimants
#   is MCAR.
```

## Task 3: Build an imputation pipeline with recipes

```{r task3-split}
set.seed(602)
split <- initial_split(health_data, prop = 0.80, strata = churned)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)
cat("Train rows:", nrow(train), " | Test rows:", nrow(test), "\n")
```

```{r task3-recipe}
rec <- recipe(churned ~ age + bmi + income + plan_tier + num_claims, data = train) |>
  step_impute_median(income) |>
  step_impute_knn(bmi, neighbors = 5)
```

```{r task3-prep-bake}
rec_prepped   <- prep(rec, training = train)
train_imputed <- bake(rec_prepped, new_data = train)
test_imputed  <- bake(rec_prepped, new_data = test)
```

## Task 4: Verify imputation success

```{r task4-verify}
train_imputed |>
  summarise(miss_bmi = sum(is.na(bmi)), miss_income = sum(is.na(income))) |>
  mutate(dataset = "train") |>
  bind_rows(
    test_imputed |>
      summarise(miss_bmi = sum(is.na(bmi)), miss_income = sum(is.na(income))) |>
      mutate(dataset = "test")
  )
```

```{r task4-compare}
before_median <- median(health_data$bmi, na.rm = TRUE)
after_median  <- median(train_imputed$bmi, na.rm = TRUE)

cat("BMI median before imputation:", round(before_median, 2), "\n")
cat("BMI median after imputation: ", round(after_median, 2), "\n")
# The medians should be nearly identical because median imputation preserves
# the central tendency, and kNN imputation borrows from similar records.
```
